ExplanationParts.CorpusEarnedOpening: Cutting the cat names Nanquan’s canonical action and functions as a later benchmark for decisive conduct.
EvidenceBody: This graph form occurs 278 times in 119 allowlisted texts and is the orthographic counterpart of “cut the cat” (斬猫), not a different event. In the records it abbreviates the public case in which the east and west halls fight over a cat; Nanquan holds it up and says, “If you can speak, I will not cut it,” the assembly gives no answer, and he cuts the cat in two. When Zhaozhou returns, he puts a sandal on his head and leaves; Nanquan says that had he been there, he would have saved the cat. The phrase functions as case narration and title, an object of questions, a subject for verses, and a cited precedent. One public exchange explicitly asks, “Killing living beings is a major precept; why did Nanquan cut the cat and Guizong cut the snake?”; Miyun Yuanwu tells the questioner to repent. Another sermon quotes the rule to rescue animals from killing and asks how Nanquan's cat and Guizong's snake could have been saved. These passages establish the corpus's own precept relation without stating Nanquan's intention. Asked for the case's import, Jueyin answers only, “It takes Nanquan” (須是南泉始得). Dahui reports and rejects students' labels “timely wondrous function” and “great function appears, not retaining rules.”
